text: Kripke argues that 'Hesperus is Phosphorus' is necessary a posteriori. What makes the identity necessary?
choices: The statement is analytic, true purely in virtue of the meanings of the two names.
The reference-fixing descriptions 'the morning star' and 'the evening star' are necessarily co-satisfied.
'Hesperus' and 'Phosphorus' are rigid designators of the same object (Venus), and identities between co-referring rigid designators hold in every world.
We can conceive of no epistemically possible world in which the morning star differs from the evening star.
explanation: Since both names rigidly designate Venus, and everything is necessarily self-identical, 'Hesperus is Phosphorus' is true in every world where the object exists (necessary), even though its truth was discovered empirically (a posteriori). Option 0 is wrong because the identity is not analytic, and option 1 misidentifies the source: the reference-fixing descriptions are non-rigid and vary across worlds, which is exactly what generates the illusion of contingency.
